# Exercise 1: Hypothesis Tests (Cycle 1)

```{r}
#| label: ex1-data
# NHANES adults: one row per participant, age 20 and over
adults <- NHANES |>
  distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  filter(Age >= 20)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex1-tests
# 1. Compare total cholesterol (TotChol, mmol/L) between physically active and
#    inactive adults (PhysActive) with t.test(). Report the two group means,
#    the 95% CI for the difference, and the p-value
# 2. Count adults with diabetes by Sex: drop rows with a missing Diabetes value,
#    then group_by(Sex) and summarize() the number with Diabetes == "Yes" and
#    the group size. Compare the two shares with prop.test(x = ..., n = ...)
# 3. Is ever smoking (Smoke100) related to BMI category (BMI_WHO)?
#    Build the two-way table with table() and run chisq.test() on it
# 4. Write one plain-language sentence for each p-value (as comments or in the
#    text below)
```

# Exercise 2: Linear Regression (Cycle 2)

```{r}
#| label: ex2-data
# Countries in 2004 (GDP_per_capita is in $1,000 per person)
gm04 <- gm |>
  filter(year == 2004, !is.na(continent),
         !is.na(life_expectancy), !is.na(sanitation))
fit_le <- lm(life_expectancy ~ sanitation, data = gm04)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex2-lm
# 1. Fit fit_gdp <- lm(life_expectancy ~ GDP_per_capita, data = gm04)
#    and look at coef(fit_gdp). Interpret the slope in words: what is the
#    difference in life expectancy for a $1,000 difference in GDP per person?
# 2. Compare the R-squared of fit_gdp with that of fit_le (sanitation model)
#    using summary(...)$r.squared. Which predictor explains more?
# 3. Plot life_expectancy against GDP_per_capita with geom_point() and
#    geom_smooth(method = "lm"). Does a straight line fit well?
# 4. In adults, fit lm(BPSysAve ~ Age + Sex + BMI). Interpret the BMI
#    coefficient. Then make "male" the reference level of Sex with
#    fct_relevel() and refit. Which coefficient changes, and how?

```
